This handout collects the theory behind Seminar 1: what an optimization problem is, derivatives of functions of one and several variables, Taylor's formula, definiteness of matrices, optimality conditions and convexity. It is written for reading from zero: a derivative from a first calculus course is all you need, and vectors, determinants, gradients, Hessians and eigenvalues are introduced on the way. Every statement comes with an example with numbers; the main proofs start with their idea in one sentence; two kinds of boxes mark the traps where almost everyone slips and short questions to check yourself. The section on seminar problems contains all eleven problems with complete solutions; the home practice, common mistakes and a glossary follow.

\begin{conventionbox}
Vectors are columns: $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^\top \in \mathbb R^n$, and $x^\top y = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n$ is a number. $\|x\| = \sqrt{x^\top x}$ is the Euclidean length. Every problem is a minimization, $\min_{x \in \Omega} f(x)$: a maximum of $f$ is a minimum of $-f$. The gradient $\nabla f(x)$ is a column vector and $H(x)$ is the Hessian; for every function in this handout $H$ is symmetric. $x^*$ denotes a candidate point or a minimizer. $A \succ 0$ and $A \succeq 0$ mean that a symmetric matrix $A$ is positive definite and positive semidefinite. A step along a direction $s$ is $x + \alpha s$ with a step parameter $\alpha \ge 0$; it is a length only when $\|s\| = 1$. The letter $\lambda$ is a weight in $[0, 1]$ or an eigenvalue, and the context always tells which.
\end{conventionbox}

\section{Notation}\label{sec:notation}

Formulas are easier to read when you can say them aloud. The table lists the symbols, how to read them and what they mean.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}l>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.23\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.53\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Symbol & How to read it & Meaning \\
\midrule
$\mathbb R^n$ & “R n” & ordered lists of $n$ real numbers, for example $x = \val{ex.notation.point} \in \mathbb R^3$ \\
$\|x\|$ & “the norm of x” & the length $\sqrt{x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2}$ \\
$x^\top y$ & “x transpose y”, “the inner product” & $x^\top$ is the column $x$ written as a row; $x^\top y = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n$ is a single number \\
$\nabla f$ & “nabla f”, “grad f” & the column of first partial derivatives \\
$\partial f/\partial x_1$ & “partial f partial x one” & the partial derivative with respect to $x_1$ \\
$H$ & “the Hessian”, “H of x” & the matrix of second partial derivatives \\
$\Omega$ & “omega” & the feasible set, where the minimum is sought \\
$x^*$ & “x star” & a candidate point or a minimizer \\
$A \succ 0$, $A \succeq 0$ & “A is positive definite”, “positive semidefinite” & $h^\top A h > 0$ for all $h \ne 0$ (all eigenvalues positive); $h^\top A h \ge 0$ for all $h$ (all eigenvalues nonnegative) \\
$o(\alpha)$ & “little o of alpha” & a quantity with $o(\alpha)/\alpha \to 0$ as $\alpha \to 0$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{notebox}{The inner product is a number}
$x = \val{ex.dot.x}$ and $y = \val{ex.dot.y}$ give $x^\top y = \val{ex.dot.x.1} \cdot \val{ex.dot.y.1} + (\val{ex.dot.x.2}) \cdot \val{ex.dot.y.2} = \val{ex.dot.value}$: a number, not a vector. In the section on optimality conditions this number becomes the rate of change of a function along a direction.
\end{notebox}

\section{Optimization problems}\label{sec:optimization}

The whole seminar tells one story. We want the points where a function takes its smallest value. Checking every point is impossible, so we learn to recognize a minimum by local signs, by the derivatives at the point itself: the first derivative produces candidates, the second one sorts them and in rare cases only a direct argument helps.

\subsection{What we minimize and why}\label{sub:optimization-problem}

An optimization problem is written as
\[
\min_{x \in \Omega} f(x).
\]
 Here $f$ is the \textbf{objective function}, $x \in \mathbb R^n$ are the \textbf{variables} and $\Omega$ is the \textbf{feasible set}, the points among which the minimum is sought. With two variables a candidate is a point of the plane, with three a point of space. With many variables there is no picture, but the formulas are the same.

In machine learning the variables are the parameters of a model, and the function is its error on the data. A linear model with \val{ex.ml.nWeights} weights is a point of $\mathbb R^{ \val{ex.ml.nWeights} }$, a neural network has about $\val{ex.ml.tex.nNet}$ parameters. With training data $(a_i, y_i)$, $i = 1, \dots, m$, a feature vector $a_i$ and a target $y_i$, \textbf{training} means minimizing the \textbf{empirical risk}
\[
L(w) = \frac1m \sum_{i=1}^m \ell\big(y_i,\ w^\top a_i\big),
\]
 where the loss $\ell$ measures the error on one object, for example $\ell(y, \hat y) = (y - \hat y)^2$.

\begin{examplebox}
Fit a line $y = w_1 + w_2 t$ to the points $(t_i, y_i)$ with $t = \val{ex.fit.t}$ and $y = \val{ex.fit.y}$. With the squared loss, training is the problem
\[
\min_{w \in \mathbb R^2} L(w), \qquad L(w) = \val{ex.fit.tex.L}.
\]
 The answer $w^* = \val{ex.fit.tex.w}$ with $L(w^*) = \val{ex.fit.tex.Lmin}$ is derived in the section on convexity, once gradients and convexity are available.
\end{examplebox}

\begin{whybox}
Brute force is hopeless: a grid with only \val{ex.ml.gridPerAxis} values per coordinate has $\val{ex.ml.tex.gridSize}$ points in $\mathbb R^{ \val{ex.ml.nWeights} }$. Instead of searching everywhere we look at one point and ask what its derivatives say.
\end{whybox}

\subsection{The feasible set}\label{sub:optimization-feasible}

The feasible set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ collects the points that are allowed. When $\Omega = \mathbb R^n$, the problem is \textbf{unconstrained}. Typical feasible sets are the quadrant $\{x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0\}$, the disk $\|x\| \le \val{ex.disk.r}$ and, in general, a set described by a system of inequalities.

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Interior and boundary points.}
A point $x \in \Omega$ is \textbf{interior} if some ball $\{y:\ \|y - x\| < \varepsilon\}$ with $\varepsilon > 0$ lies in $\Omega$; otherwise it is a \textbf{boundary} point.
\end{definitionbox}

\begin{examplebox}
In the quadrant $\Omega = \{x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0\}$ the point $\val{ex.quadrant.interior}$ is interior. The point $\val{ex.quadrant.boundary}$ is a boundary point: a step to the left, however small, leaves $\Omega$. The corner $\val{ex.quadrant.corner}$ is a boundary point too. This distinction becomes decisive in the section on optimality conditions.
\end{examplebox}

\subsection{Local and global minima}\label{sub:optimization-minima}

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Local minimum.}
A point $x^* \in \Omega$ is a \textbf{local minimum} of $f$ on $\Omega$ if there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that
\[
f(x) \ge f(x^*) \quad \text{for all } x \in \Omega \text{ with } \|x - x^*\| < \varepsilon.
\]

\end{definitionbox}

Read the definition clause by clause. “There is $\varepsilon > 0$”: some radius exists, possibly a very small one. “For all $x \in \Omega$ with $\|x - x^*\| < \varepsilon$”: $x^*$ is compared only with feasible points closer than this radius. “$f(x) \ge f(x^*)$”: none of them is lower, and equal values are allowed. In short, $x^*$ is a lowest feasible point in some neighbourhood of itself.

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Global minimum.}
A point $x^* \in \Omega$ is a \textbf{global minimum} of $f$ on $\Omega$ if $f(x) \ge f(x^*)$ for all $x \in \Omega$, with no restriction on the distance.
\end{definitionbox}

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Strict minimum.}
A minimum is \textbf{strict} if $f(x) > f(x^*)$ for every admissible $x \ne x^*$: for all $x \in \Omega$ with $0 < \|x - x^*\| < \varepsilon$ in a \textbf{strict local minimum} and for all $x \in \Omega$ with $x \ne x^*$ in a \textbf{strict global minimum}.
\end{definitionbox}

\begin{examplebox}
$f(x) = x_1^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$ satisfies $f \ge 0$ everywhere and $f = 0$ on the whole line $x_1 = 0$. Every point of this line is a global minimum, and none of them is strict, because each has neighbours on the line with the same value. Such a line is a flat bottom.
\end{examplebox}

\begin{notebox}{Local and global}
A global minimum is a local one whose neighbourhood is all of $\Omega$. Derivatives are local tools; a global claim needs convexity, a direct bound or, when a global minimum is known to exist (for example when $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $\|x\| \to \infty$, or when $\Omega$ is closed and bounded), a comparison of all local minima.
\end{notebox}

\begin{selfcheckbox}
A function on the line tends to $+\infty$ as $|x| \to \infty$ and has two wells of different depth. How many local and how many global minima does it have?
\selfcheckanswer Two local minima and one global, at the bottom of the deeper well; a global minimum exists because $f$ grows at infinity. If the two wells have equal depth, both bottoms are global minima; each is still a strict local minimum, but neither is a strict global minimum.
\end{selfcheckbox}

\section{Warm-up: one variable}\label{sec:one-variable}

We start with the derivative from a first calculus course and look at it with the eyes of optimization.

\subsection{The derivative is a rate}\label{sub:one-variable-derivative}

The \textbf{derivative} of $f:\ \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ at a point $x$ is the limit
\[
f'(x) = \lim_{\alpha \to 0} \frac{f(x + \alpha) - f(x)}{\alpha}.
\]
 Take a small step $\alpha$ and divide the change of $f$ by the step: the result is a rate, the change of $f$ per unit of step. Geometrically, $f'(x)$ is the slope of the tangent to the graph at $x$. A one-sided version, with $\alpha \to 0^+$, appears with directional derivatives.

If $f'(x) \ne 0$ at a point inside the domain, then $f$ decreases on one side of $x$, so $x$ is not a minimum.

\subsection{A zero derivative is necessary, not sufficient}\label{sub:one-variable-stationary}

\begin{examplebox}
$f(x) = x^3$ has $f'(x) = \val{ex.cubic.tex.fprime}$ and $f'(0) = 0$, yet $f < 0$ to the left of $0$ and $f > 0$ to the right: $0$ is no extremum.
\end{examplebox}

\handoutfigure{0.95}{fig_stationary}{Left: $x^3$ has $f'(0) = 0$ but no extremum. Middle: $x^2$ has a strict minimum at $0$. Right: $f(x) = \val{ex.wells.tex.f}$ with $f'(x) = \val{ex.wells.tex.fprime}$ has local minima at $x = \val{ex.wells.stationary.1}$ and $x = \val{ex.wells.stationary.3}$ and a local maximum at $x = \val{ex.wells.stationary.2}$; only the deeper well, $f(\val{ex.wells.stationary.3}) = \val{ex.wells.values.3}$, is the global minimum.}

\begin{notebox}{Necessary and sufficient}
A condition is \textbf{necessary} if it holds at every minimum, and \textbf{sufficient} if it guarantees a minimum. At interior points $f'(x) = 0$ is necessary but not sufficient: solving $f' = 0$ gives candidates, not answers.
\end{notebox}

The second derivative tells $x^2$ from $x^3$: for $x^2$ it gives $f''(0) = \val{ex.square.second} > 0$, while for $x^3$ it gives $f''(0) = 0$, which carries no information.

\subsection{Taylor's formula}\label{sub:one-variable-taylor}

\textbf{Taylor's formula} replaces a function near a point by a polynomial. For a twice differentiable $f$,
\[
f(x + \alpha) = \underbrace{f(x)}_{\text{value}} + \underbrace{f'(x)\,\alpha}_{\text{linear part}} + \underbrace{\tfrac12 f''(x)\,\alpha^2}_{\text{curvature}} + o(\alpha^2).
\]
 The remainder $o(\alpha^2)$ satisfies $o(\alpha^2)/\alpha^2 \to 0$ as $\alpha \to 0$: for small steps it is negligible next to the other terms.

\begin{notebox}{How to use it}
If $f'(x) \ne 0$, the linear term decides: a small step with $f'(x)\alpha < 0$ decreases $f$, so $x$ is not a minimum. If $f'(x) = 0$, the sign of $f''(x)$ decides: $f''(x) > 0$ gives a strict local minimum and $f''(x) < 0$ a strict local maximum. If also $f''(x) = 0$, the formula is silent. The section on Taylor's formula in several variables repeats this logic for many variables.
\end{notebox}

\begin{examplebox}
For $f(x) = \val{ex.wells.tex.f}$ we have $f'(x) = \val{ex.wells.tex.fprime}$ and $f''(x) = \val{ex.wells.tex.fsecond}$. At the stationary points: $f''(\val{ex.wells.stationary.1}) = \val{ex.wells.second.1} > 0$, a local minimum; $f''(\val{ex.wells.stationary.2}) = \val{ex.wells.second.2} < 0$, a local maximum; $f''(\val{ex.wells.stationary.3}) = \val{ex.wells.second.3} > 0$, a local minimum. Which of the two minima is global the derivatives do not say. Since $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $|x| \to \infty$, a global minimum exists and is one of the local minima, so compare the values $f(\val{ex.wells.stationary.1}) = \val{ex.wells.values.1}$ and $f(\val{ex.wells.stationary.3}) = \val{ex.wells.values.3}$.
\end{examplebox}

\begin{selfcheckbox}
Let $f(x) = x^4$. Find $f'(0)$ and $f''(0)$. Is $0$ a minimum?
\selfcheckanswer Both are zero, so the test is silent. But $x^4 \ge 0$ for every $x$ with equality only at $0$, so $0$ is a strict global minimum. The same situation returns in two variables in problem B4.
\end{selfcheckbox}

\section{Functions of several variables}\label{sec:multivariate}

A function of $n$ variables assigns a number to every point of $\mathbb R^n$. The examples of this section use the function from the lecture, $f = \val{ex.lecture.tex.f}$, at the point $\val{ex.lecture.point}$; problem A2 evaluates the same function at another point.

\subsection{Level sets: a height map}\label{sub:multivariate-level-sets}

A function of two variables is easy to picture as a relief: $f(x_1, x_2)$ is the height above the point $(x_1, x_2)$. The \textbf{level set} $\{x:\ f(x) = c\}$ collects the points of equal height $c$, exactly like a contour line on a topographic map. Several level sets drawn with their values give a height map of $f$. Two different level sets never cross, because a point has only one height.

\handoutfigure{0.95}{fig_level_sets}{Level sets with their values. Left: $x_1^2 + x_2^2$ (problem B1), circles around a minimum. Middle: $x_1^2 + x_2^2 - x_1x_2$ (problem A1), tilted ellipses around a minimum. Right: $x_1^2 - x_2^2$ (problem B2), hyperbolas around a saddle; the dashed lines are the level $0$.}

Closed nested level sets surround a pit or a hill, and only the level values tell which: without them a pit and a hill look the same. Open level sets that turn away from each other mark a saddle: the function goes up in one direction and down in another. Where level sets with evenly spaced values crowd together, the function changes fast.

\subsection{Partial derivatives}\label{sub:multivariate-partial}

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Partial derivative.}
The \textbf{partial derivative} of $f$ with respect to $x_i$ is the ordinary derivative in $x_i$ with all other variables held fixed; it is the rate of change of $f$ when only $x_i$ moves:
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(x) = \lim_{\alpha \to 0} \frac{f(x_1, \dots, x_i + \alpha, \dots, x_n) - f(x)}{\alpha}.
\]

\end{definitionbox}

In practice: treat every letter except $x_i$ as a number and differentiate by the usual rules. The result is again a function of all $n$ variables.

\begin{examplebox}
Differentiate $f = \val{ex.lecture.tex.f}$ term by term. With respect to $x_1$: $\val{ex.lecture.tex.term1}$ gives $\val{ex.lecture.tex.d1term1}$; in $\val{ex.lecture.tex.term2}$ the factor $x_2^2$ is a “number”, so the term gives $\val{ex.lecture.tex.d1term2}$; $\val{ex.lecture.tex.term3}$ does not contain $x_1$ and gives $0$. So $\partial f/\partial x_1 = \val{ex.lecture.tex.g1}$. Likewise, with respect to $x_2$ the first term gives $0$ and the other two give $\val{ex.lecture.tex.d2term2}$ and $\val{ex.lecture.tex.d2term3}$, so $\partial f/\partial x_2 = \val{ex.lecture.tex.g2}$.
\end{examplebox}

\begin{selfcheckbox}
Find both partial derivatives of $f = \val{ex.partial.tex.f}$.
\selfcheckanswer $\partial f/\partial x_1 = \val{ex.partial.tex.g1}$ and $\partial f/\partial x_2 = \val{ex.partial.tex.g2}$.
\end{selfcheckbox}

\subsection{The gradient}\label{sub:multivariate-gradient}

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Gradient.}
The \textbf{gradient} of $f$ at $x$ collects all partial derivatives into one column vector:
\[
\nabla f(x) = \big(\partial f/\partial x_1, \dots, \partial f/\partial x_n\big)^\top \in \mathbb R^n.
\]

\end{definitionbox}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent}, and $-\nabla f$ in the direction of steepest descent. Its length $\|\nabla f\|$ is the rate of change in that direction per unit of length (when $\nabla f(x) \ne 0$). This is why gradient descent steps against the gradient; the section on optimality conditions proves it with the directional derivative.
  \item \textbf{The gradient is perpendicular to level sets.} Along a level set $f$ does not change, so its rate of change in that direction is zero, and the gradient has no component along the level set.
\end{itemize}

\handoutfigure{0.5}{fig_gradient}{Level sets of $f = \val{ex.dir.tex.f}$ and the point $P = \val{ex.dir.point}$ on the level $f = \val{ex.dir.f}$. The gradient $\nabla f(P) = \val{ex.dir.grad}$ is perpendicular to this level set and points uphill; $-\nabla f(P)$ points downhill; along the tangent direction $\tau$ the rate of change is zero. The direction $s = \val{ex.dir.s}$ of problem D2 makes an obtuse angle with $\nabla f(P)$, so $f$ decreases along it.}

\begin{examplebox}
Evaluating the partial derivatives of the lecture function at the point gives $\nabla f\val{ex.lecture.point} = (\val{ex.lecture.g1parts.1} + \val{ex.lecture.g1parts.2},\ \val{ex.lecture.g2parts.1} + \val{ex.lecture.g2parts.2})^\top = \val{ex.lecture.grad}$. A small step $\alpha$ along $\val{ex.lecture.grad}$ changes $f$ by about $\alpha\,(\val{ex.lecture.gradSq.1} + \val{ex.lecture.gradSq.2}) = \val{ex.lecture.rate}\alpha$; the opposite step decreases $f$ by the same amount to first order. The factor in front of $\alpha$ is $\|\nabla f\|^2$, the inner product of the gradient with itself.
\end{examplebox}

\subsection{The Hessian}\label{sub:multivariate-hessian}

Differentiating a partial derivative again, in the same or in another variable, gives a second partial derivative. For $n$ variables there are $n^2$ of them, and they are arranged in a square table.

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Hessian.}
The \textbf{Hessian} of $f$ at $x$ is the $n \times n$ matrix of second partial derivatives; its entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is $\partial^2 f/\partial x_i\,\partial x_j$:
\[
H(x) = \big[\partial^2 f/\partial x_i\,\partial x_j\big]_{i,j=1}^n.
\]

\end{definitionbox}

\begin{theorembox}{Theorem: Schwarz.}
If the second partial derivatives of $f$ are continuous, they do not depend on the order of differentiation: $\partial^2 f/\partial x_i\,\partial x_j = \partial^2 f/\partial x_j\,\partial x_i$. Hence the Hessian is symmetric.
\end{theorembox}

All functions of the seminar are polynomials, whose second derivatives are continuous everywhere, so their Hessians are symmetric. This matters: everything later, eigenvalues and Sylvester's criterion included, is about symmetric matrices.

\begin{examplebox}
The Hessian of the lecture function step by step. Differentiating $\partial f/\partial x_1 = \val{ex.lecture.tex.g1}$ in $x_1$ gives $\val{ex.lecture.tex.h11}$ and in $x_2$ gives $\val{ex.lecture.tex.h12}$; differentiating $\partial f/\partial x_2 = \val{ex.lecture.tex.g2}$ in $x_2$ gives $\val{ex.lecture.tex.h22}$. So
\[
H(x) = \val{ex.lecture.tex.H}, \qquad H\val{ex.lecture.point} = \val{ex.lecture.H},
\]
 and $\det H\val{ex.lecture.point} = \val{ex.lecture.detProd} - \val{ex.lecture.offSq} = \val{ex.lecture.det}$. Check the symmetry: differentiating $\partial f/\partial x_2$ in $x_1$ gives the same $\val{ex.lecture.tex.h12}$. Unlike the Hessian of a quadratic function, this one depends on the point, so problem A2 gets a different matrix at its point.
\end{examplebox}

\subsection{The cross-term trap}\label{sub:multivariate-cross-term}

\begin{trapbox}
A term $c\,x_1x_2$ gives $H_{12} = H_{21} = c$: differentiate directly, $\partial(c\,x_1x_2)/\partial x_1 = c\,x_2$ and then $\partial(c\,x_2)/\partial x_2 = c$, with no halving. The value $c/2$ is the entry of $A$ in $f = x^\top A x$: the product $x^\top A x$ produces $x_1x_2$ twice, as $A_{12}x_1x_2 + A_{21}x_2x_1$, and $H = A + A^\top$ for a symmetric $A$. The form $f = \tfrac12 x^\top H x$ needs no halving. The two wrong values seen in practice are $c/2$ (the $x^\top A x$ convention) and $2c$ (doubling as if the term were a square).
\end{trapbox}

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Convention & Off-diagonal entry & For $f = \val{ex.cross.tex.f}$ \\
\midrule
Hessian $H$ & $c$ & $H_{12} = \val{ex.cross.H12}$ \\
$f = x^\top A x$ & $c/2$ & $A_{12} = \val{ex.cross.A12}$ \\
$f = \tfrac12 x^\top H x$ & $c$ & the Hessian itself \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The rule for reading $H$ off a polynomial of degree two without differentiating: the diagonal holds twice the coefficient of each square; each cross term puts its coefficient into both symmetric positions; variables that never appear together give $0$.

\begin{selfcheckbox}
Write down the Hessian of $f = \val{ex.hess3.tex.f}$ without differentiating term by term.
\selfcheckanswer The diagonal holds twice the coefficients of the squares, the off-diagonal entries hold the coefficients of the cross terms in both symmetric positions; $x_1$ and $x_3$ never meet:
\[
H = \val{ex.hess3.H}.
\]

\end{selfcheckbox}

\section{Taylor's formula in several variables}\label{sec:taylor}

Taylor's formula is the main tool of the course: near a point a smooth function is replaced by a polynomial with a small error, and every optimality condition is read off this formula.

\subsection{The formula}\label{sub:taylor-formula}

For a twice continuously differentiable $f$ and a small vector $h$, the value near $x$ is the value at $x$ plus a linear and a quadratic term, up to a small remainder:
\[
f(x + h) = f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top h + \tfrac12\, h^\top H(x)\, h + o(\|h\|^2).
\]
 The remainder satisfies $o(\|h\|^2)/\|h\|^2 \to 0$ as $h \to 0$.

\begin{itemize}
  \item $f(x)$: the value where we stand, the starting height.
  \item $\nabla f(x)^\top h$: the \textbf{linear part}, a single number, the inner product of the gradient with the shift. It changes sign with $h$: the steps $h$ and $-h$ have linear parts of equal size and opposite signs.
  \item $\tfrac12 h^\top H h$: the \textbf{quadratic part}, the curvature. It is unchanged under $h \to -h$, because $h$ enters twice.
\end{itemize}

\begin{whybox}
If $\nabla f(x) \ne 0$, the linear part dominates for small steps, and one of $h$ and $-h$ decreases $f$, so $x$ is not a minimum. If $\nabla f(x) = 0$, the linear part vanishes and the sign of $h^\top H h$ over all directions $h$ decides; the section on quadratic forms and definiteness studies these signs.
\end{whybox}

\subsection{Computing the quadratic term}\label{sub:taylor-quadratic-form}

The number $h^\top H h$ is built from the entries of $H$ and the components of $h$. For $n = 2$, multiplying out gives
\[
h^\top H h = H_{11}h_1^2 + 2H_{12}h_1h_2 + H_{22}h_2^2.
\]
 Such a sum of squares and products of the components with constant coefficients is called a \textbf{quadratic form}. The cross term appears twice, as $H_{12}h_1h_2$ and $H_{21}h_2h_1$, hence the factor $2$: the same doubling as in the cross-term trap.

\begin{examplebox}
For the lecture Hessian $H = \val{ex.lecture.H}$ and the step $h = \val{ex.lecture.h}$: $h^\top H h = \val{ex.lecture.hHh}$ and $\tfrac12 h^\top H h = \val{ex.lecture.halfhHh}$.
\end{examplebox}

\subsection{A numerical check}\label{sub:taylor-numerical}

Numbers show that the formula really works. Take the lecture function at $\val{ex.lecture.point}$, where $f = \val{ex.lecture.f}$, $\nabla f = \val{ex.lecture.grad}$ and $H = \val{ex.lecture.H}$. Along $h = t\,\val{ex.lecture.h}$ compare three numbers: the exact value, the linear model $\val{ex.taylor.tex.lin}$ and the quadratic model $\val{ex.taylor.tex.quad}$.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$t$ & exact $f$ & linear & quadratic & linear error & quadratic error \\
\midrule
$\val{ex.taylor.half.t}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.half.tex.exact}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.half.tex.lin}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.half.tex.quad}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.half.tex.errLin}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.half.tex.errQuad}$ \\
$\val{ex.taylor.tenth.t}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.tenth.tex.exact}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.tenth.tex.lin}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.tenth.tex.quad}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.tenth.tex.errLin}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.tenth.tex.errQuad}$ \\
$\val{ex.taylor.hundredth.t}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.hundredth.tex.exact}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.hundredth.tex.lin}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.hundredth.tex.quad}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.hundredth.tex.errLin}$ & $\val{ex.taylor.hundredth.tex.errQuad}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Dividing $t$ by $\val{ex.taylor.stepRatio}$, as from the second row to the third, divides the linear error by about $\val{ex.taylor.linFactor}$ (like $t^2$) and the quadratic error by $\val{ex.taylor.quadFactor}$ (like $t^3$). Along this line $f$ equals $\val{ex.taylor.tex.along}$, so the quadratic error is exactly $\val{ex.taylor.tex.remainder}$. This is what $o(\|h\|^2)$ means: the remainder vanishes faster than the terms that are written out.

\begin{notebox}{Quadratic functions: the formula is exact}
A polynomial of degree two has no nonzero third derivatives, so the remainder is zero and Taylor's formula is exact. Check it on $q = \val{ex.quad.tex.f}$ at $\val{ex.quad.point}$: $q = \val{ex.quad.f}$, $\nabla q = \val{ex.quad.grad}$, $H = \val{ex.quad.H}$. For $h = \val{ex.quad.h}$ the linear part is $\val{ex.quad.linear}$; the products $h_1^2$, $h_1h_2$ and $h_2^2$, equal to $\val{ex.quad.hSq}$, give $h^\top H h = \val{ex.quad.hHh}$ and the quadratic part $\val{ex.quad.quadratic}$. The total is $\val{ex.quad.value}$, equal to $q\val{ex.quad.shifted}$. Linear regression with the squared loss is quadratic in the weights, so it is solved by a formula, without iterations.
\end{notebox}

\section{Quadratic forms and definiteness}\label{sec:definiteness}

Taylor's formula shows that at a point with $\nabla f(x) = 0$ the linear term vanishes and the quadratic term $\tfrac12\,h^\top H(x)\,h$ takes over. Whether $f$ goes up or down near $x$ therefore depends on the signs that $h^\top H h$ takes as $h$ ranges over all directions. This section studies which signs a quadratic form can take and how to find them.

\subsection{Five cases}\label{sub:definiteness-cases}

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Definiteness.}
Let $A$ be a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix. $A$ is \textbf{positive definite}, $A \succ 0$, if $h^\top A h > 0$ for all $h \ne 0$, and \textbf{positive semidefinite}, $A \succeq 0$, if $h^\top A h \ge 0$ for all $h$. $A$ is \textbf{negative definite}, $A \prec 0$, if $h^\top A h < 0$ for all $h \ne 0$, and \textbf{negative semidefinite}, $A \preceq 0$, if $h^\top A h \le 0$ for all $h$. Finally, $A$ is \textbf{indefinite} if $h^\top A h$ takes both signs: $h^\top A h > 0$ for some $h$ and $g^\top A g < 0$ for some $g$.
\end{definitionbox}

In terms of a landscape, the graph of $h^\top A h$ is a bowl when $A \succ 0$, a dome when $A \prec 0$, a saddle when $A$ is indefinite and a trough with a flat bottom when $A \succeq 0$ is singular: along the directions with $h^\top A h = 0$ the graph stays at height $0$.

\handoutfigure{1}{fig_definiteness}{Level sets of $h^\top A h$: a bowl for $A = \val{ex.eig.pd.A}$, a dome for $A = \val{ex.defFig.nd}$, a saddle for $A = \val{ex.eig.indef.A}$ and a trough for $A = \val{ex.defFig.psd}$, whose zero eigenvalue gives the flat bottom drawn in red.}

\subsection{Eigenvalues give the answer}\label{sub:definiteness-eigenvalues}

A symmetric $n \times n$ matrix $A$ has $n$ mutually perpendicular unit \textbf{eigenvectors} $v_1, \dots, v_n$: along each of them $A$ acts as a stretch, $Av_i = \lambda_i v_i$, and the stretch factors $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ are the \textbf{eigenvalues}, all of them real. Write $h$ in the axes of the eigenvectors, $h = u_1v_1 + \dots + u_nv_n$. Then the cross terms disappear and the quadratic form becomes a weighted sum of squares:
\[
h^\top A h = \lambda_1u_1^2 + \dots + \lambda_nu_n^2.
\]
 Every question about the signs of $h^\top A h$ is now answered by the signs of the $\lambda_i$.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Eigenvalues & Type & Level sets \\
\midrule
all $> 0$ & positive definite & ellipses around a minimum \\
all $< 0$ & negative definite & ellipses around a maximum \\
both signs & indefinite & hyperbolas, a saddle \\
all $\ge 0$, some zero & positive semidefinite & parallel lines, a trough \\
all $\le 0$, some zero & negative semidefinite & the same, upside down \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix the eigenvalues are the roots of the quadratic equation $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$, that is
\[
\lambda^2 - (A_{11} + A_{22})\lambda + \det A = 0.
\]


\begin{examplebox}
$A = \val{ex.eig.pd.A}$: the equation is $\val{ex.eig.pd.tex.poly} = 0$ with the roots $\val{ex.eig.pd.values}$, both positive, so $A$ is positive definite. $A = \val{ex.eig.indef.A}$: the equation is $\val{ex.eig.indef.tex.poly} = 0$ with the roots $\val{ex.eig.indef.values}$ of opposite signs, so $A$ is indefinite. These are the Hessians of problems A1 and C2.
\end{examplebox}

The two matrices differ only in the size of the off-diagonal entry. So a cross term can destroy definiteness, and what decides is its size, not its sign: changing the sign of the off-diagonal entries of a $2 \times 2$ matrix does not change its eigenvalues. Problem C2 studies the whole family.

\begin{notebox}{Looking ahead: the condition number}
For $A \succ 0$ the ratio $\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$ is the \textbf{condition number}; it measures how stretched the level sets are. For $x_1^2 + x_2^2$ the eigenvalues are $\val{ex.kappa.bowl.eig}$, so $\kappa = \val{ex.kappa.bowl.value}$ and the level sets are circles: a gradient step with step size $\val{ex.kappa.bowl.tex.step}$ lands exactly at the minimum, $x - \val{ex.kappa.bowl.tex.step} \cdot 2x = 0$. For the matrix of problem A1, $\kappa = \val{ex.kappa.pd.value}$ and the level sets are ellipses. The larger $\kappa$, the narrower the ravine and the slower gradient methods: the later topics of the course return to this.
\end{notebox}

\subsection{Sylvester's criterion}\label{sub:definiteness-sylvester}

For a $\val{ex.syl.nLeading} \times \val{ex.syl.nLeading}$ matrix the eigenvalues are the roots of a cubic equation, which is unpleasant to solve by hand. Strict definiteness can be checked with determinants instead. For a $2 \times 2$ matrix $\det \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc$, and a larger one is expanded along a row, as in the example below; the determinant equals the product of the eigenvalues, so $\det A < 0$ already makes $A$ indefinite.

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Leading principal minor.}
The \textbf{leading principal minor} $\Delta_k$ of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is the determinant of the submatrix formed by the first $k$ rows and the first $k$ columns of $A$, $k = 1, \dots, n$. They are usually called just the \textbf{leading minors}.
\end{definitionbox}

\begin{examplebox}
$A = \val{ex.syl.A}$: $\Delta_1 = \val{ex.syl.minors.1}$, $\Delta_2 = \val{ex.syl.d2prod.1} - \val{ex.syl.d2prod.2} = \val{ex.syl.minors.2}$ and $\Delta_3 = \det A = \val{ex.syl.A.1.1} \cdot \val{ex.syl.cof.1} - \val{ex.syl.A.1.2} \cdot \val{ex.syl.cof.2} + 0 = \val{ex.syl.terms.1} - \val{ex.syl.terms.2} = \val{ex.syl.minors.3}$ (expansion along the first row). All three minors are positive, so the criterion below gives $A \succ 0$.
\end{examplebox}

\begin{theorembox}{Theorem: Sylvester's criterion.}
Let $A$ be a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix. Then
\[
A \succ 0 \iff \Delta_k > 0 \text{ for all } k, \qquad A \prec 0 \iff (-1)^k\Delta_k > 0 \text{ for all } k.
\]
 The second pattern means alternating signs starting with minus: $\Delta_1 < 0$, $\Delta_2 > 0$, $\Delta_3 < 0$ and so on.
\end{theorembox}

\emph{Why it works}, for $2 \times 2$ and $A_{11} \ne 0$: complete the square,
\[
A_{11}h_1^2 + 2A_{12}h_1h_2 + A_{22}h_2^2 = A_{11}\big(h_1 + \tfrac{A_{12}}{A_{11}}h_2\big)^2 + \tfrac{\Delta_2}{\Delta_1}h_2^2.
\]
 If $\Delta_1 = A_{11} > 0$ and $\Delta_2 > 0$, both coefficients are positive, and the sum vanishes only when $h_2 = 0$ and then $h_1 = 0$. If $\Delta_1 < 0$ and $\Delta_2 > 0$, both coefficients are negative. In general Gaussian elimination does the same: it completes the squares one variable at a time, and the leading minors control the signs of the coefficients that appear.

\subsection{What Sylvester's criterion cannot do}\label{sub:definiteness-limits}

\begin{trapbox}
Sylvester's criterion speaks only about strict definiteness. If neither pattern holds, do not conclude that the matrix is indefinite: it may be semidefinite. $A = \val{ex.sylTrap.A}$ and $B = \val{ex.sylTrap.B}$ have the same leading minors, $(\Delta_1, \Delta_2) = \val{ex.sylTrap.minors}$, but $A \preceq 0$ and $B \succeq 0$. The same minors give opposite answers, so the leading minors cannot decide semidefiniteness at all.
\end{trapbox}

A correct test of semidefiniteness uses \textbf{all} principal minors: $A \succeq 0$ exactly when the determinants of all submatrices on a set of rows and the same set of columns are nonnegative. A $\val{ex.syl.nLeading} \times \val{ex.syl.nLeading}$ matrix has $\val{ex.syl.nLeading}$ leading but $\val{ex.syl.nPrincipal}$ principal minors; for the matrix $A$ above they are $\val{ex.syl.principal}$. For $\operatorname{diag}(0, -1)$ the principal minors are $\val{ex.sylTrap.principalA}$, and the negative one shows that it is not $\succeq 0$.

\begin{notebox}{A practical rule}
On paper, use Sylvester's criterion only to decide strict definiteness. If some $\Delta_k = 0$, compute the eigenvalues instead; for a $2 \times 2$ matrix this is one quadratic equation. In code, always compute the eigenvalues and compare them with zero using a tolerance, because floating-point arithmetic rarely produces an exact zero (see the section “From the board to the keyboard”).
\end{notebox}

\begin{selfcheckbox}
Check $A = \val{ex.sylCheck.A}$ with Sylvester's criterion. What can you conclude?
\selfcheckanswer $(\Delta_1, \Delta_2) = \val{ex.sylCheck.minors}$. The pattern of $A \succ 0$ needs every $\Delta_k > 0$ and fails at $\Delta_2$; the pattern of $A \prec 0$ needs $\Delta_1 < 0$ and fails at once. Neither pattern holds, so the criterion only says that $A$ is not definite. The eigenvalues $\val{ex.sylCheck.eig}$ have opposite signs and show that the matrix is indefinite.
\end{selfcheckbox}

\section{Optimality conditions}\label{sec:optimality}

Taylor's formula, definiteness and the difference between interior and boundary points now combine into four statements: a lemma on the directional derivative and three optimality conditions. Together they are the core of the first lecture of the course.

\subsection{Feasible directions}\label{sub:optimality-directions}

From an interior point of $\Omega$ you can move a little in any direction and stay in $\Omega$. From a boundary point you cannot: some directions leave $\Omega$ at once.

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Feasible direction.}
A vector $s \in \mathbb R^n$, $s \ne 0$, is a \textbf{feasible direction} at a point $x \in \Omega$ if there is $\alpha_0 > 0$ such that $x + \alpha s \in \Omega$ for all $\alpha \in [0, \alpha_0]$.
\end{definitionbox}

In words: a small enough step along $s$ keeps the point feasible. The number $\alpha_0$ may be tiny, but it must be positive.

\handoutfigure{0.95}{fig_feasible}{Feasible directions in the quadrant $\Omega = \{x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0\}$. At the boundary point $P = \val{ex.quadrant.boundary}$ they form the half-plane $s_1 \ge 0$ (problem D1), at the corner $Q = \val{ex.quadrant.corner}$ the quarter $s_1 \ge 0,\ s_2 \ge 0$ (home practice H3) and at the interior point $R = \val{ex.quadrant.interior}$ every direction is feasible. The dashed red directions leave $\Omega$ at once.}

If $s$ is feasible, so is $ts$ for every $t > 0$: the feasible directions form a \textbf{cone}. For a convex $\Omega$ they form, together with $0$, a convex cone; for a nonconvex $\Omega$ they need not. At the origin of $\{x_1 \le 0\} \cup \{x_2 \le 0\}$ the feasible directions are $\{s \ne 0:\ s_1 \le 0 \text{ or } s_2 \le 0\}$, and this set is not convex even with $0$ added.

\subsection{The directional derivative}\label{sub:optimality-directional}

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Directional derivative.}
Let $x \in \Omega$ and let $s$ be a direction. The \textbf{directional derivative} of $f$ at $x$ along $s$ is the one-sided limit
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(x) = \lim_{\alpha \to 0^+} \frac{f(x + \alpha s) - f(x)}{\alpha}.
\]

\end{definitionbox}

This is the ordinary derivative from a first calculus course, with the step taken along the vector $s$ instead of along an axis. The limit is one-sided because at a boundary point only steps with $\alpha \ge 0$ may be allowed. At an interior point of a differentiable $f$ both one-sided limits exist and agree, so the two-sided limit is not a mistake there.

\begin{theorembox}{Lemma: The directional derivative through the gradient.}
If $f$ is differentiable at $x$, then $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s}(x) = s^\top\nabla f(x)$ for every direction $s$.
\end{theorembox}

\begin{proofbox}
Put $h = \alpha s$ into Taylor's formula:
\[
f(x + \alpha s) = f(x) + \alpha\,s^\top\nabla f(x) + o(\alpha).
\]
 Subtract $f(x)$, divide by $\alpha > 0$ and let $\alpha \to 0^+$: the term $o(\alpha)/\alpha$ tends to $0$, and $s^\top\nabla f(x)$ remains.
\end{proofbox}

\begin{notebox}{Why this lemma matters}
A limit, which takes work to compute, becomes an inner product, which takes one line. The lemma also explains why the gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent: among directions of length $1$, the rate $s^\top\nabla f$ is largest for $s = \nabla f/\|\nabla f\|$ (when $\nabla f \ne 0$), where it equals $\|\nabla f\|$, because $s^\top\nabla f \le \|s\|\,\|\nabla f\|$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
\end{notebox}

\begin{examplebox}
$f = \val{ex.dir.tex.f}$, $x = \val{ex.dir.point}$, $s = \val{ex.dir.s}$. The gradient is $\nabla f = \val{ex.dir.tex.grad}$, at $x$ it equals $\val{ex.dir.grad}$, so $s^\top \nabla f(x) = \val{ex.dir.value}$: $f$ decreases along $s$. The fastest decrease per unit length is along $-\nabla f(x)/\|\nabla f(x)\|$, with rate $-\|\nabla f(x)\| = \val{ex.dir.tex.steepest} \approx \val{ex.dir.steepest}$, about $\val{ex.dir.ratio}$ times the rate along $s/\|s\|$ (see the trap below). This is why gradient descent steps against the gradient.
\end{examplebox}

\begin{trapbox}
The number $\val{ex.dir.value}$ is a rate per unit of $\alpha$, not per unit of length. Here $\|s\| = \val{ex.dir.tex.norm} \approx \val{ex.dir.norm}$, so per unit length the rate is $\val{ex.dir.value}/\|s\| = \val{ex.dir.tex.perLength} \approx \val{ex.dir.perLength}$. Compare directions only after normalizing them; otherwise the longest vector looks the steepest.
\end{trapbox}

\subsection{The first-order necessary condition}\label{sub:optimality-first-order}

\begin{theorembox}{Theorem: First-order necessary condition.}
Let $f \in C^1$ on $\Omega$ and let $x^*$ be a local minimum of $f$ on $\Omega$. Then
\[
s^\top\nabla f(x^*) \ge 0
\]
 for every feasible direction $s$ at $x^*$. If, in addition, $x^*$ is an interior point of $\Omega$, then $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$.
\end{theorembox}

\begin{whybox}
If $f$ decreased along a direction in which you are allowed to move, a small step in that direction would give a feasible point with a smaller value, and $x^*$ would not be a minimum.
\end{whybox}

\begin{proofbox}
Suppose that $s$ is feasible and $s^\top\nabla f(x^*) = -\delta < 0$. By Taylor's formula
\[
f(x^* + \alpha s) = f(x^*) - \alpha\delta + o(\alpha),
\]
 and $|o(\alpha)| < \tfrac12\alpha\delta$ for all small $\alpha > 0$. For these $\alpha$
\[
f(x^* + \alpha s) < f(x^*) - \alpha\delta + \tfrac12\alpha\delta = f(x^*) - \tfrac12\alpha\delta < f(x^*).
\]
 For small $\alpha$ the point $x^* + \alpha s$ lies in $\Omega$, because $s$ is feasible, and is as close to $x^*$ as needed: a contradiction with the local minimality of $x^*$. Hence $s^\top\nabla f(x^*) \ge 0$. At an interior point both $s$ and $-s$ are feasible for every $s \ne 0$, so $s^\top\nabla f(x^*) \ge 0$ and $-s^\top\nabla f(x^*) \ge 0$, that is $s^\top\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ for all $s$. The only vector orthogonal to every vector is zero, so $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$.
\end{proofbox}

\begin{notebox}{In plain words}
From a minimum you cannot go downhill in any direction in which you are allowed to move. The familiar condition $\nabla f = 0$ is not a separate theorem but the special case of an interior point: there you may move both ways along every line, and “not downhill both ways” means “flat”. In Seminar 2 this inequality becomes the KKT conditions.
\end{notebox}

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Stationary point.}
A point $x$ with $\nabla f(x) = 0$ is a \textbf{stationary point} of $f$. Stationary points are the candidates for an unconstrained minimum: by the theorem above, a local minimum at an interior point is always stationary.
\end{definitionbox}

\subsection{The second-order necessary condition}\label{sub:optimality-second-necessary}

\begin{theorembox}{Theorem: Second-order necessary condition.}
Let $f \in C^2$ on $\Omega$, let $x^*$ be a local minimum of $f$ on $\Omega$ and let $s$ be a feasible direction at $x^*$ with $s^\top\nabla f(x^*) = 0$. Then $s^\top H(x^*)\,s \ge 0$. In particular, at an interior point $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ and $H(x^*) \succeq 0$.
\end{theorembox}

\begin{whybox}
When the linear term of Taylor's formula vanishes along $s$, the quadratic term takes over, so the curvature along $s$ decides. Negative curvature along $s$ would mean that $f$ goes down along $s$.
\end{whybox}

\begin{proofbox}
Put $h = \alpha s$ into Taylor's formula; the linear term vanishes because $s^\top\nabla f(x^*) = 0$:
\[
f(x^* + \alpha s) = f(x^*) + \tfrac12\alpha^2\,s^\top H s + o(\alpha^2), \qquad H = H(x^*).
\]
 If $s^\top H s = -\delta < 0$, then $|o(\alpha^2)| < \tfrac14\alpha^2\delta$ for all small $\alpha > 0$, and for these $\alpha$
\[
f(x^* + \alpha s) < f(x^*) - \tfrac12\alpha^2\delta + \tfrac14\alpha^2\delta = f(x^*) - \tfrac14\alpha^2\delta < f(x^*).
\]
 As in the previous proof, the point $x^* + \alpha s \in \Omega$ lies arbitrarily close to $x^*$, which contradicts the local minimality of $x^*$.
\end{proofbox}

\subsection{The second-order sufficient condition}\label{sub:optimality-second-sufficient}

\begin{theorembox}{Theorem: Second-order sufficient condition.}
Let $f \in C^2$ and let $x^*$ be an \textbf{interior} point of $\Omega$ with $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ and $H(x^*) \succ 0$. Then $x^*$ is a strict local minimum.
\end{theorembox}

\begin{whybox}
A positive definite Hessian means positive curvature in all directions at once, with a margin $\mu = \lambda_{\min} > 0$, and this margin beats the remainder of Taylor's formula.
\end{whybox}

\begin{proofbox}
Let $H = H(x^*)$ and $\mu = \lambda_{\min}(H) > 0$. In the axes of the eigenvectors $h^\top H h = \lambda_1u_1^2 + \dots + \lambda_nu_n^2 \ge \mu\|h\|^2$. Since $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$, Taylor's formula gives
\[
f(x^* + h) - f(x^*) = \tfrac12\,h^\top H h + o(\|h\|^2) \ge \tfrac12\mu\|h\|^2 + o(\|h\|^2).
\]
 There is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that the ball $\|h\| < \varepsilon$ around $x^*$ lies in $\Omega$ and $|o(\|h\|^2)| < \tfrac14\mu\|h\|^2$ for $0 < \|h\| < \varepsilon$. For these $h$
\[
f(x^* + h) - f(x^*) > \tfrac14\mu\|h\|^2 > 0.
\]
 So every other point of this neighbourhood has a larger value: $x^*$ is a strict local minimum.
\end{proofbox}

\subsection{Summary and procedure}\label{sub:optimality-summary}

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}l>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.51\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.27\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Order & Necessary & Sufficient \\
\midrule
first order & $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ at an interior point; $s^\top \nabla f(x^*) \ge 0$ for every feasible $s$ at a boundary point & none \\
second order & $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ and $H(x^*) \succeq 0$ at an interior point & $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ and $H(x^*) \succ 0$ at an interior point \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

There is no sufficient condition of first order. The gradient only measures the slope, and the slope is zero at a minimum, at a maximum and at a saddle alike: $x_1^2 + x_2^2$, $-x_1^2 - x_2^2$ and $x_1^2 - x_2^2$ all have $\nabla f(0) = 0$. Telling them apart needs information about the curvature.

\begin{notebox}{The procedure}
First find the candidates, the points where $\nabla f = 0$, and compute $H$ at each of them. If $H \succ 0$, the candidate is a strict local minimum; if $H \prec 0$, a strict local maximum; if $H$ is indefinite, a saddle. If $H$ is singular and semidefinite, the second-order test cannot decide, and $f$ itself has to be analysed near the point. Finally, call a minimum global only with an extra argument: convexity or a bound from below.
\end{notebox}

\subsection{The gap between semidefinite and definite}\label{sub:optimality-gap}

Between the necessary and the sufficient condition of second order there is a gap: $H \succeq 0$ but not $H \succ 0$, a semidefinite Hessian with a zero eigenvalue. It may seem that the theory is just weak here and that a sharper test could close the gap. It cannot: no criterion that uses only $\nabla f$ and $H$ at the point can close it, and the next example proves this.

\begin{notebox}{Same data, different answers}
$f_1 = \val{ex.gap.tex.f1}$ and $f_2 = \val{ex.gap.tex.f2}$ both have $\nabla f(0) = 0$ and $H(0) = 0$. Yet $f_1$ has a strict global minimum at the origin, while $f_2$ has no extremum there (problems B4 and B3). The data of first and second order are the same and the correct answers differ, so no test that sees only $\nabla f(0)$ and $H(0)$ can tell the two functions apart.
\end{notebox}

In such a case, return to the definition of a minimum and work with $f$ itself. One of two techniques usually helps:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Bound from below.} $f_1 = \val{ex.gap.tex.f1} \ge 0 = f_1(0)$, with equality only at the origin, so the origin is a strict global minimum. One line, no derivatives.
  \item \textbf{Find a direction of decrease.} Restrict $f_2$ to the line $x_2 = 0$: $f_2(x_1, 0) = x_1^3$ changes sign at $0$. So arbitrarily close to the origin $f_2$ takes both positive and negative values, and the origin is not an extremum.
\end{itemize}

\handoutfigure{0.8}{fig_monkey}{Left: the sign of $f_2 = \val{ex.gap.tex.f2}$ around the origin, \val{ex.monkey.nSectors} sectors of $\val{ex.monkey.sectorDeg}^\circ$ where $f_2 > 0$ (blue) and $f_2 < 0$ (red) alternate. Right: $f_1 = \val{ex.gap.tex.f1}$ is positive everywhere except the origin. Both functions have $\nabla f(0) = 0$ and $H(0) = 0$.}

\begin{selfcheckbox}
Let $g(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Find its stationary points and its Hessian. What does the theory say about these points?
\selfcheckanswer $\nabla g = \val{ex.flat.tex.grad}$ vanishes on the whole line $x_1 = 0$, and $H = \val{ex.flat.H} \succeq 0$ but not $\succ 0$, so the sufficient condition does not apply. Still, $g \ge 0$ and $g = 0$ on the line, so every point of the line is a non-strict global minimum: the flat bottom of a trough.
\end{selfcheckbox}

\subsection{Why the monkey saddle has six sectors}\label{sub:optimality-monkey-saddle}

The graph of $f_2 = \val{ex.gap.tex.f2}$ is the monkey saddle, and its picture can be explained completely. In polar coordinates $x_1 = r\cos\varphi$, $x_2 = r\sin\varphi$ the function becomes $f_2 = \val{ex.monkey.tex.step1}$. Replacing $\sin^2\varphi$ by $1 - \cos^2\varphi$ and using the triple-angle identity $\val{ex.monkey.tex.identity}$ gives
\[
f_2 = \val{ex.monkey.tex.step2} = \val{ex.monkey.tex.step3} = \val{ex.monkey.tex.polar}.
\]
 The factor $r^3$ is positive for $r > 0$, so the sign of $f_2$ depends only on the angle $\varphi$: going once around the circle, the cosine factor changes sign \val{ex.monkey.nSectors} times. This gives \val{ex.monkey.nSectors} sectors of $\val{ex.monkey.sectorDeg}^\circ$, \val{ex.monkey.nUp} going up and \val{ex.monkey.nDown} going down.

\begin{whybox}
An ordinary saddle has two descending sectors, one for each leg of a rider. This one has three: room for the two legs and the tail of a sitting monkey, hence the name.
\end{whybox}

\begin{selfcheckbox}
How many sign sectors does $f = \val{ex.octo.tex.f}$ have around the origin, and what does the second-order test say there?
\selfcheckanswer In polar coordinates $f = \val{ex.octo.tex.polar}$, so the sign changes \val{ex.octo.nSectors} times around the circle: \val{ex.octo.nSectors} sectors. The origin is the only stationary point and $H(0) = 0$, so the test gives no verdict; the sign changes show that the origin is not an extremum.
\end{selfcheckbox}

\section{Convexity}\label{sec:convexity}

Convexity is the one widely available property that turns local statements into global ones, which is why both theory and machine learning hold on to it.

\subsection{Convex sets}\label{sub:convexity-sets}

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Convex set.}
A set $\Omega$ is \textbf{convex} if together with any two of its points it contains the whole segment between them: $\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) y \in \Omega$ for all $x, y \in \Omega$ and $\lambda \in [0, 1]$.
\end{definitionbox}

The point $\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) y$ runs over the segment from $y$ ($\lambda = 0$) to $x$ ($\lambda = 1$); $\lambda = \tfrac12$ gives the midpoint. A proof of convexity must show that the segment stays inside for every pair of points; to disprove convexity, one pair whose segment leaves the set is enough, as for the ring in the figure.

\handoutfigure{1}{fig_convexity}{From left to right: the disk $\|x\| \le \val{ex.disk.r}$ is convex (problem C1); the ring $\val{ex.ring.r.1} \le \|x\| \le \val{ex.ring.r.2}$ is not, because the red part of the segment crosses the hole; $x^2$ is a convex function, its chord lies above the graph; $(x^2 - 1)^2$ is not convex, the chord between its two minima lies below the graph.}

\begin{examplebox}
Every ball $\{x:\ \|x - c\| \le r\}$ in every norm is convex, including the $\ell_1$ diamond and the $\ell_\infty$ square, which have corners. The proof in problem C1 uses only the triangle inequality and homogeneity of the norm: convexity is not smoothness.
\end{examplebox}

\subsection{Convex functions}\label{sub:convexity-functions}

\begin{definitionbox}{Definition: Convex function.}
A function $f$ on a convex set $\Omega$ is \textbf{convex} if
\[
f\big(\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) y\big) \le \lambda f(x) + (1 - \lambda) f(y)
\]
 for all $x, y \in \Omega$ and $\lambda \in [0, 1]$. It is \textbf{strictly convex} if the inequality is strict whenever $x \ne y$ and $0 < \lambda < 1$.
\end{definitionbox}

The left side is the value of the function at a point of the segment, the right side is the value on the chord that joins the endpoints of the graph: the graph never rises above a chord. In particular, $f$ is convex along every line: for fixed $x$ and $s$ the function of one variable $t \mapsto f(x + ts)$ is convex where it is defined, so a single line along which this function is not convex shows that $f$ is not convex.

\begin{theorembox}{Theorem: Second-order criterion.}
Let $f \in C^2$ on an open convex set $\Omega$. Then $f$ is convex $\iff H(x) \succeq 0$ for all $x \in \Omega$. If $H(x) \succ 0$ for all $x \in \Omega$, then $f$ is strictly convex.
\end{theorembox}

The converse of the last part fails: $f(x) = x^4$ is strictly convex, yet $f''(0) = 0$. It is the same gap between $\succeq$ and $\succ$ as in the optimality conditions.

\begin{selfcheckbox}
Is $f = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + a\,x_1x_2$ convex for $a = \val{ex.family.a}$?
\selfcheckanswer No. The Hessian $H = \val{ex.family.H}$ has the eigenvalues $2 \pm a$, that is $\val{ex.family.eig}$; one of them is negative, so $f$ is not convex. It is convex exactly for $|a| \le \val{ex.family.bound}$ (problem C2).
\end{selfcheckbox}

\subsection{Every local minimum is global}\label{sub:convexity-local-global}

\begin{theorembox}{Theorem: Local minimum of a convex function.}
If $f$ is convex on a convex set $\Omega$ and $x^*$ is a local minimum, then $x^*$ is a global minimum.
\end{theorembox}

\begin{whybox}
A better point far away would pull the whole chord, and with it the graph, below $f(x^*)$, so points arbitrarily close to $x^*$ would be better too.
\end{whybox}

\begin{proofbox}
Suppose $f(y) < f(x^*)$ for some $y \in \Omega$ and put $z_\lambda = \lambda y + (1 - \lambda)x^*$, which lies in $\Omega$ because $\Omega$ is convex. Convexity of $f$ gives $f(z_\lambda) \le \lambda f(y) + (1 - \lambda) f(x^*)$, that is $f(z_\lambda) \le f(x^*) - \lambda\big(f(x^*) - f(y)\big) < f(x^*)$ for $\lambda \in (0, 1]$, while $\|z_\lambda - x^*\| = \lambda\|y - x^*\| \to 0$ as $\lambda \to 0$. So arbitrarily close to $x^*$ there are points with a smaller value: a contradiction with local minimality.
\end{proofbox}

\begin{theorembox}{Corollary.}
For a convex $f \in C^1$ on $\mathbb R^n$, the equality $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ is not only necessary but also sufficient for a global minimum.
\end{theorembox}

\begin{proofbox}
Let $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ and suppose $f(y) < f(x^*)$ for some $y$. Put $s = y - x^*$ and $\varphi(\lambda) = f(x^* + \lambda s)$. By convexity $\varphi(\lambda) \le (1 - \lambda)\varphi(0) + \lambda\varphi(1)$, so $\frac{\varphi(\lambda) - \varphi(0)}{\lambda} \le \varphi(1) - \varphi(0) < 0$ for all $\lambda \in (0, 1]$. Letting $\lambda \to 0^+$ gives $s^\top \nabla f(x^*) \le f(y) - f(x^*) < 0$, which contradicts $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$.
\end{proofbox}

\subsection{Why this matters in machine learning}\label{sub:convexity-ml}

The empirical risk with a regularization term, $L(w) = \frac1m \sum_i \ell(y_i,\ w^\top a_i) + \rho\|w\|^2$ with $\rho \ge 0$, is convex whenever the loss $\ell$ is convex in its second argument: a composition with the affine map $w \mapsto w^\top a_i$ and a nonnegative sum keep convexity. The squared loss, the logistic loss and the Huber loss are convex, so for linear models every point with zero gradient is a global minimizer. A neural network loses this property already with one hidden layer, which is why people speak about its loss landscape.

\begin{examplebox}
The line fit from the section on optimization problems: $L(w) = \frac1m\|Xw - y\|^2$ with $m = \val{ex.fit.n}$ and $X = \val{ex.fit.X}$. Then $\nabla L(w) = \frac2m X^\top(Xw - y)$ and $H_L = \frac2m X^\top X = \val{ex.fit.tex.H}$, the same at every $w$. Its entry $H_{11}$ is positive and $\det H_L = \val{ex.fit.tex.detH} > 0$, so $H_L \succ 0$ and $L$ is strictly convex. The condition $\nabla L = 0$ is the \textbf{normal equation} $X^\top X w = X^\top y$, here $\val{ex.fit.XtX}\, w = \val{ex.fit.Xty}$, and its solution $w^* = \val{ex.fit.tex.w}$ is the unique global minimizer, $L(w^*) = \val{ex.fit.tex.Lmin}$. With collinear features $X^\top X$ is singular, $H_L$ is only semidefinite and the minimizer is no longer unique; the regularization term $\rho\|w\|^2$ adds $2\rho I$ to $H_L$.
\end{examplebox}

\begin{whybox}
For a convex loss, a method that drives the gradient to zero has found the answer; for a nonconvex loss it has found a candidate.
\end{whybox}

\section{From the board to the keyboard}\label{sec:numerics}

Every statement of the seminar has a short numerical counterpart. Two functions are enough: an independent check of a gradient formula and a second-order test with a tolerance; they are the starting point of home practice H4. The notebook of this seminar checks every number of this handout by two independent computations.

\subsection{Checking a gradient: central differences}\label{sub:numerics-gradient}

\begin{codebox}
\begin{lstlisting}[style=handoutcode]
def central_diff(f, x, h=1e-5):
    """Gradient by central differences: an independent check of an analytic formula."""
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    g = np.empty_like(x)
    for j in range(x.size):
        e = np.zeros_like(x)
        e[j] = h
        g[j] = (f(x + e) - f(x - e)) / (2 * h)
    return g
\end{lstlisting}
\end{codebox}

\texttt{central\_diff} approximates each partial derivative by a central difference,
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}(x) \approx \frac{f(x + he_j) - f(x - he_j)}{2h},
\]
 with an error of order $h^2$; here $e_j$ is the $j$-th coordinate vector.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{The check must be independent}: if the difference reuses parts of the analytic gradient, it checks itself.
  \item \textbf{The step has an optimum}: the truncation error $\sim h^2$ competes with the rounding error $\sim \varepsilon_{\text{mach}}/h$, so the best step is $h \sim \varepsilon_{\text{mach}}^{1/3} \approx \val{ex.fd.tex.hOpt}$ with $\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} \approx \val{ex.fd.tex.eps}$, hence the default $h = \val{ex.fd.tex.h}$.
  \item \textbf{Symmetrize} a numerical Hessian before \texttt{eigvalsh}, which reads only one triangle of the matrix.
\end{itemize}

\begin{examplebox}
For the lecture function at $\val{ex.lecture.point}$, \texttt{central\_diff} returns $\val{ex.fd.gradLecture}$ up to an error below $\val{ex.fd.tex.tol}$, in agreement with the formula for $\nabla f$.
\end{examplebox}

\subsection{Classifying a Hessian with a tolerance}\label{sub:numerics-classify}

\begin{codebox}
\begin{lstlisting}[style=handoutcode]
def classify(H, rel_tol=1e-9):
    """Second-order test for a symmetric matrix: "min", "max", "saddle" or "inconclusive".

    It reads the matrix only, so call it at a stationary point. The tolerance is relative to the largest |eigenvalue|.
    """
    H = np.asarray(H, dtype=float)
    w = np.linalg.eigvalsh(0.5 * (H + H.T))
    tol = rel_tol * np.abs(w).max(initial=0.0)
    if np.all(w > tol):
        return "min"
    if np.all(w < -tol):
        return "max"
    if w.min() < -tol and w.max() > tol:
        return "saddle"
    return "inconclusive"
\end{lstlisting}
\end{codebox}

\texttt{classify} reads the signs of the eigenvalues of the symmetrized matrix with a tolerance relative to the largest absolute eigenvalue, so rescaling the matrix does not change the answer. A matrix that is zero up to rounding has no scale: build Hessians exactly, by hand or with sympy, before calling it; a finite-difference Hessian of $f_1 = \val{ex.gap.tex.f1}$ at the origin is classified as \texttt{"min"}.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}rll@{}}
\toprule
Matrix & Where it comes from & Output \\
\midrule
$\val{ex.classify.bowl.H}$ & problem B1 at the origin & \texttt{"min"} \\
$\val{ex.classify.saddle.H}$ & problem B2 at the origin & \texttt{"saddle"} \\
$\val{ex.classify.zero.H}$ & problems B3 and B4 at the origin & \texttt{"inconclusive"} \\
$\val{ex.classify.halfSaddle.H}$ & home practice H1 at the origin & \texttt{"inconclusive"} \\
$\val{ex.classify.nsd.H}$ & the Sylvester trap & \texttt{"inconclusive"} \\
$\val{ex.classify.notStationary.H}$ & problem A2 at $\val{ex.classify.notStationary.point}$ & \texttt{"min"} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{trapbox}
\texttt{classify} looks at a matrix, not at a point. For the function of problem A2 at $\val{ex.classify.notStationary.point}$ it returns \texttt{"min"}, because $H = \val{ex.classify.notStationary.H} \succ 0$, yet $\nabla f = \val{ex.classify.notStationary.grad} \ne 0$: the point is not even stationary. Check the gradient first.
\end{trapbox}

\begin{trapbox}
Do not write the saddle test as the chained comparison \texttt{w.min() < -tol < w.max()}. It means \texttt{w.min() < -tol and -tol < w.max()}, which is also true when the largest eigenvalue is $0$: the matrix $\operatorname{diag}(0, -1)$, which is negative semidefinite, would be called a saddle. A saddle needs \texttt{w.min() < -tol and w.max() > tol}.
\end{trapbox}

The two \texttt{"inconclusive"} answers for B3 and B4 are not a weakness of the code: from $\nabla f$ and $H$ alone the mathematics cannot decide (see the subsection on the gap between semidefinite and definite).

\section{Questions students ask}\label{sec:faq}

\faqquestion{Why do we need necessary conditions if they prove nothing?}
They turn an infinite search into a finite one: instead of checking every feasible point, solve $\nabla f = 0$ and check the candidates. A point that violates a necessary condition is ruled out at once. Numerical methods follow the same idea: every gradient-based method of the first part of the course drives $\nabla f$ towards zero.

\faqquestion{Why not just look at the graph?}
For $n \le 2$ you can, and the pictures of this handout do. For a linear model with \val{ex.ml.nWeights} weights or a network with about $\val{ex.ml.tex.nNet}$ parameters there is no graph to look at, while the formulas work in any dimension. Even in the plane a picture can mislead: without level values a pit and a hill look the same. A picture gives intuition; a proof is a bound or a restriction to a line.

\faqquestion{Is the Hessian always symmetric?}
For the functions of this course, yes: by Schwarz's theorem the mixed second derivatives are equal when they are continuous, and counterexamples need discontinuous second derivatives. In code, symmetrize anyway: in a numerical Hessian the entries $H_{ij}$ and $H_{ji}$ differ in the last digits, and \texttt{eigvalsh} reads only one triangle.

\faqquestion{What does $o(\alpha)$ mean, and can we do without it?}
It is the precise way to say “an error negligible for small $\alpha$”, precise enough to prove theorems with: $g(\alpha) = o(\alpha)$ means $g(\alpha)/\alpha \to 0$ as $\alpha \to 0$. For example, $f(x + h) = f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top h + o(\|h\|)$ states that the error of the linear approximation vanishes faster than $\|h\|$. Without it every statement would be approximate.
