\section{Seminar problems}\label{sec:problems}

All eleven problems with complete solutions, grouped by the four blocks of the seminar. In each block the first problem is worked through in class and the others are for solving on your own.

\subsection{A. Gradients and Hessians}\label{sub:problems-a}

\problemhead{A1}{Gradient and Hessian of a quadratic}{Partial derivatives term by term; a cross term in both off-diagonal entries}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $f(x) = \val{A1.tex.f}$. \textbf{(a)} Before computing: will the Hessian $H$ depend on the point? \textbf{(b)} Find $\nabla f$ and $H$ at an arbitrary point and at $\val{A1.params.x}$. \textbf{(c)} Is $\val{A1.params.x}$ a candidate for a minimum?

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item Differentiate term by term. For $x_1$: $x_1^2$ gives $2x_1$, $x_2^2$ gives nothing, $-x_1x_2$ gives $-x_2$. So $\partial f/\partial x_1 = \val{A1.tex.g1}$ and, in the same way, $\partial f/\partial x_2 = \val{A1.tex.g2}$.
  \item Second derivatives:
\[
H = \val{A1.steps.H}.
\]
 No variable is left: the Hessian of a quadratic is constant. The cross term $-x_1x_2$ puts $-1$ into \textbf{both} off-diagonal entries.
  \item At $\val{A1.params.x}$: $\nabla f = \val{A1.steps.grad} \ne 0$. The point is not stationary, so it is not a candidate for an unconstrained minimum, whatever $H$ says.
  \item The eigenvalues solve $\val{A1.tex.charPoly} = 0$: $\lambda = \val{A1.steps.eig.1}$ and $\lambda = \val{A1.steps.eig.2}$. Both are positive at every point, so $f$ is strictly convex and its unique minimizer solves $\nabla f = 0$: $x^* = \val{A1.steps.xStar}$.
  \item Two conventions, one function: $f = \tfrac12 x^\top H x$ with $H$ itself, or $f = x^\top A x$ with $A = \val{A1.tex.A}$, whose off-diagonal entry is $\val{A1.tex.offA}$; $H = A + A^\top$. Mixing the two is what produces wrong Hessians.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
$\nabla f = (\val{A1.tex.g1},\ \val{A1.tex.g2})^\top$, $H = \val{A1.steps.H}$ at every point; $\nabla f\val{A1.params.x} = \val{A1.steps.grad} \ne 0$, so $\val{A1.params.x}$ is not a candidate.
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{A2}{The Hessian moves with the point}{Substitution with signs; curvature of a non-quadratic function is local}
\textbf{Statement.} For the lecture function $f(x) = \val{A2.tex.f}$ compute $\nabla f$, $H$ and $\det H$ at $\val{A2.params.x}$. Compare with $\det H = \val{A.lecture.det}$ at $\val{A.lecture.x}$. Is $\val{A2.params.x}$ a stationary point?

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item Differentiate: $\partial f/\partial x_1 = \val{A2.tex.g1}$, $\partial f/\partial x_2 = \val{A2.tex.g2}$ and
\[
H(x) = \val{A2.tex.H}.
\]

  \item Keep the numbers visible: $\partial f/\partial x_1 = \val{A2.tex.sub1} = \val{A2.steps.grad.1}$ and $\partial f/\partial x_2 = \val{A2.tex.sub2} = \val{A2.steps.grad.2}$, a sum of two negative terms. $H\val{A2.params.x} = \val{A2.steps.H}$: both off-diagonal entries are negative.
  \item $\det H = \val{A2.tex.detSub} = \val{A2.steps.det}$, against $\val{A.lecture.det}$ at $\val{A.lecture.x}$. For a non-quadratic function the curvature is a local object.
  \item No: $\nabla f\val{A2.params.x} = \val{A2.steps.grad} \ne 0$, so the point is not stationary. $H \succ 0$ ($\Delta_1 = \val{A2.steps.H.1.1} > 0$, $\Delta_2 = \val{A2.steps.det} > 0$) says nothing about optimality at a non-stationary point.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
$\nabla f = \val{A2.steps.grad}$, $H = \val{A2.steps.H}$, $\det H = \val{A2.steps.det}$; the point is not stationary.
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{A3}{Three variables and Sylvester's criterion}{A three-by-three Hessian, leading minors, the minimizer of a convex quadratic}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $f(x) = \val{A3.tex.f}$ on $\mathbb R^3$. \textbf{(a)} Find $\nabla f$ and $H$. \textbf{(b)} Decide by Sylvester's criterion whether $H \succ 0$. \textbf{(c)} What does this say about convexity? Where is the minimum, and is it unique?

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item The diagonal holds twice the coefficients of the squares, $\val{A3.steps.diag}$. The term $2x_1x_2$ gives $H_{12} = H_{21} = \val{A3.steps.H.1.2}$, the term $-x_2x_3$ gives $H_{23} = H_{32} = \val{A3.steps.H.2.3}$, and $x_1$, $x_3$ never meet, so $H_{13} = 0$:
\[
\nabla f = \val{A3.tex.grad},\qquad H = \val{A3.steps.H}.
\]

  \item $\Delta_1 = \val{A3.steps.minors.1}$, $\Delta_2 = \val{A3.tex.delta2} = \val{A3.steps.minors.2}$ and, expanding along the first row, $\Delta_3 = \val{A3.tex.delta3} = \val{A3.steps.minors.3}$.
  \item All leading minors are positive, so $H \succ 0$. The Hessian is the same at every point, so $f$ is strictly convex on $\mathbb R^3$.
  \item Solve $\nabla f = 0$: $\val{A3.tex.system}$, hence $\val{A3.tex.loop}$, so $x_2 = 0$ and then $x_3 = x_1 = 0$. The unique stationary point $x^* = \val{A3.steps.xStar}$ is the global minimizer by convexity.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
$H = \val{A3.steps.H}$, $\Delta = \val{A3.steps.minors}$, so $H \succ 0$ and $f$ is strictly convex; the unique global minimizer is $x^* = \val{A3.steps.xStar}$.
\end{answerbox}

\subsection{B. Classifying stationary points}\label{sub:problems-b}

\problemhead{B1}{A bowl: local first, global separately}{The full routine: stationary point, Hessian, sufficient condition, a separate global argument}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $f(x) = \val{B1.tex.f}$. \textbf{(a)} Find all stationary points. \textbf{(b)} Compute $H$ and decide its definiteness. \textbf{(c)} Which condition did you use: necessary or sufficient? \textbf{(d)} Is the point a global minimum, and what exactly justifies that?

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item $\nabla f = \val{B1.tex.grad} = 0$ only at $x^* = \val{B1.steps.xStar}$.
  \item $H = \val{B1.steps.H}$ with $\Delta_1 = \val{B1.steps.minors.1} > 0$ and $\Delta_2 = \val{B1.steps.minors.2} > 0$, so $H \succ 0$.
  \item $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$ and $H(x^*) \succ 0$: the \textbf{sufficient} condition applies, and it gives a \textbf{strict local} minimum, nothing more.
  \item Global needs one more sentence: either convexity ($H \succeq 0$ at every point) or directly $f(x) = \val{B1.tex.f} \ge 0 = f(x^*)$, with equality only at $x^*$.
  \item The eigenvalues $\val{B1.steps.eig.1}$ and $\val{B1.steps.eig.2}$ are equal: the curvature is the same in every direction and the level sets are circles. Gradient descent with the step size $\val{B1.tex.step}$ reaches $x^*$ in one step from any $x$: $x - \val{B1.tex.step}\nabla f(x) = 0$.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
The only stationary point is $x^* = \val{B1.steps.xStar}$; $H \succ 0$ gives a strict local minimum by the sufficient condition; it is global because $f \ge 0 = f(x^*)$ (or by convexity).
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{B2}{A saddle, proved without a picture}{Indefinite Hessian; restriction to two lines as the proof}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $f(x) = \val{B2.tex.f}$. Show that $(0, 0)$ is a stationary point that is neither a minimum nor a maximum, without using a picture.

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item $\nabla f = \val{B2.tex.grad}$ vanishes only at the origin, and $H = \val{B2.steps.H}$.
  \item $\Delta_1 = \val{B2.steps.minors.1} > 0$ and $\Delta_2 = \val{B2.steps.minors.2} < 0$: neither. Since $\det H < 0$, the eigenvalues $\val{B2.steps.eig.1}$ and $\val{B2.steps.eig.2}$ have opposite signs, and $H$ is indefinite.
  \item The proof restricts $f$ to the two axes: $f(t, 0) = t^2 > 0$ and $f(0, t) = -t^2 < 0$ for $t \ne 0$. Every neighbourhood of the origin contains larger and smaller values than $f(0, 0) = 0$: a saddle.
  \item Along the line at angle $\theta$: $f(t\cos\theta, t\sin\theta) = \val{B2.tex.line}$, which vanishes identically at $\theta = \val{B2.tex.zeroAngles}$ and has opposite signs on the two sides of these lines. The picture is a guide; the two restrictions are the proof.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
$\Delta_1 = \val{B2.steps.minors.1}$, $\Delta_2 = \val{B2.steps.minors.2}$, $H$ indefinite; $f(t, 0) = t^2$ and $f(0, t) = -t^2$, so the origin is a saddle.
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{B3}{The monkey saddle}{A zero Hessian: every optimality condition is silent, the definition decides}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $f(x) = \val{B3.tex.f}$. \textbf{(a)} Find all stationary points. \textbf{(b)} Evaluate the Hessian at the origin. \textbf{(c)} Try the optimality conditions: what do they say? \textbf{(d)} Find a direction that settles the question.

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item $\partial f/\partial x_1 = \val{B3.tex.g1}$, $\partial f/\partial x_2 = \val{B3.tex.g2}$. Case split: $\val{B3.tex.g2} = 0$ gives $x_1 = 0$ \textbf{or} $x_2 = 0$, and in either case the first equation forces the other coordinate to vanish. The only stationary point is the origin.
  \item $H(x) = \val{B3.tex.H}$, so $H(0, 0) = \val{B3.steps.H0}$, the zero matrix.
  \item The zero matrix is $\succeq 0$, so the necessary condition for a minimum holds; it is also $\preceq 0$, so the one for a maximum holds too. The sufficient condition needs $H \succ 0$ and does not apply, and all $\Delta_k = 0$, so Sylvester is silent. Every tool is silent.
  \item Use the definition along a line: $f(t, 0) = t^3$ is positive for $t > 0$ and negative for $t < 0$. Every neighbourhood of the origin has larger and smaller values: neither a minimum nor a maximum.
  \item Why “monkey”: in polar coordinates $f = \val{B3.tex.polar}$, so the sign alternates in six sectors of $\val{B3.tex.sector}$, three up and three down: two valleys for the legs and one for the tail. Along $\theta = \val{B3.tex.zeroAngles}$ the function is identically zero, and those lines settle nothing.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
The only stationary point is the origin; $H(0) = 0$, so the second-order test gives no verdict; $f(t, 0) = t^3$ changes sign, so the origin is neither a minimum nor a maximum.
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{B4}{Same data, opposite answer}{A direct bound decides where the second-order test cannot}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $f(x) = \val{B4.tex.f}$. \textbf{(a)} Find the stationary points and $H(0, 0)$. \textbf{(b)} What does the second-order test say? \textbf{(c)} Decide the question in one line. \textbf{(d)} Compare with B3: what is identical and what is different?

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item $\nabla f = \val{B4.tex.grad} = 0$ only at the origin, and $H(x) = \val{B4.tex.H}$, so $H(0, 0) = \val{B4.steps.H0}$ again.
  \item The second-order test is silent again: the necessary conditions hold and the sufficient one does not apply.
  \item One line: $f(x) = \val{B4.tex.f} \ge 0 = f(0, 0)$, with equality only at the origin. A \textbf{strict global} minimum, no theorem needed.
  \item B3 and B4 have identical $\nabla f(0)$ and $H(0)$ and opposite answers. When $H(0)$ is singular and semidefinite, the second-order test provably cannot decide: two functions with the same first- and second-order data behave differently.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
$H(0, 0) = 0$ and the test is silent; $f \ge 0 = f(0, 0)$ with equality only at the origin, so it is a strict global minimum. B3 has the same $\nabla f(0)$ and $H(0)$ and no extremum.
\end{answerbox}

\subsection{C. Convexity}\label{sub:problems-c}

\problemhead{C1}{A disk is convex: a proof from the definition}{A convexity proof with a named reason on every line}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $\Omega = \{x \in \mathbb R^2:\ \val{C1.tex.set}\}$. \textbf{(a)} Prove from the definition that $\Omega$ is convex. \textbf{(b)} Which properties of the norm did the proof use? \textbf{(c)} Does the argument work for a square? For a ring?

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item Rewrite the set as a ball: $\Omega = \{x:\ \|x\| \le \val{C1.params.r}\}$. Take $x, y \in \Omega$, $\lambda \in [0, 1]$ and $z = \lambda x + (1 - \lambda) y$.
  \item
\[
\|z\| \overset{(1)}{\le} \|\lambda x\| + \|(1 - \lambda) y\| \overset{(2)}{=} \lambda\|x\| + (1 - \lambda)\|y\| \le \val{C1.params.r}\lambda + \val{C1.params.r}(1 - \lambda) = \val{C1.params.r},
\]
 where (1) is the triangle inequality and (2) is homogeneity; $\lambda$ and $1 - \lambda$ are nonnegative, so no absolute values appear. Hence $z \in \Omega$. $\blacksquare$
  \item The proof used only the triangle inequality and homogeneity: nothing about circles, the dimension or smoothness. So every ball in every norm is convex, including the $\ell_1$ diamond and the $\ell_\infty$ square, which have corners.
  \item The ring $\{\val{C1.tex.ring}\}$ is not convex: the points $\val{C1.params.ringP}$ and $\val{C1.params.ringQ}$ lie in it, but their midpoint $\val{C1.steps.ringMid}$ lies in the hole.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
Convex, by the triangle inequality and homogeneity; the same proof covers the $\ell_\infty$ square, while the ring is not convex.
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{C2}{It is the size of the cross term that matters}{Convexity of a quadratic from one constant matrix; a one-parameter family}
\textbf{Statement.} \textbf{(a)} Is $f(x) = \val{C2.tex.f}$ convex on $\mathbb R^2$? \textbf{(b)} Compare with A1, where the cross coefficient was $\val{C2.params.aA1}$. \textbf{(c)} For which $a$ is $f_a(x) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + a\,x_1x_2$ convex, and for which is it strictly convex?

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item $H = \val{C2.steps.H}$ at every point; $\Delta_1 = \val{C2.steps.minors.1} > 0$ and $\Delta_2 = \val{C2.tex.delta2} = \val{C2.steps.minors.2} < 0$.
  \item $\Delta_2 = \det H < 0$, so the eigenvalues $\val{C2.steps.eig.1}$ and $\val{C2.steps.eig.2}$ have opposite signs and $H$ is indefinite (that neither Sylvester pattern holds would not be enough). $H$ is nowhere $\succeq 0$, so $f$ is \textbf{not} convex.
  \item The family: $H_a = \val{C2.tex.Ha}$ with eigenvalues $\val{C2.tex.eigA}$. Convex $\iff$ both are $\ge 0$ $\iff |a| \le \val{C2.params.aEdge}$; strictly convex $\iff |a| < \val{C2.params.aEdge}$ — for a quadratic the converse of the second-order criterion does hold, and the next step shows what happens at $|a| = \val{C2.params.aEdge}$.
  \item $f = \val{C2.tex.fEdge}$: convex but not strictly, the eigenvalues are $\val{C2.steps.eigEdge.1}$ and $\val{C2.steps.eigEdge.2}$, and the whole line $x_1 + x_2 = 0$ consists of minimizers. A1 has $a = \val{C2.params.aA1}$ (eigenvalues $\val{C2.steps.eigA1.1}$, $\val{C2.steps.eigA1.2}$, convex); here $a = \val{C2.params.a}$: the size of the cross term decides, not its sign.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
$\Delta_2 = \val{C2.steps.minors.2}$, eigenvalues $\val{C2.steps.eig.1}$ and $\val{C2.steps.eig.2}$: not convex. $f_a$ is convex for $|a| \le \val{C2.params.aEdge}$ and strictly convex for $|a| < \val{C2.params.aEdge}$.
\end{answerbox}

\subsection{D. Feasible directions}\label{sub:problems-d}

\problemhead{D1}{Optimality on the boundary}{Active constraints, the set of feasible directions and one violating direction}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $\Omega = \{x:\ x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0\}$, $f(x) = \val{D1.tex.f}$ and $x = \val{D1.params.x}$. \textbf{(a)} Which constraints are active at $x$? \textbf{(b)} Describe all feasible directions at $x$. \textbf{(c)} Check the first-order necessary condition $s^\top \nabla f(x) \ge 0$. \textbf{(d)} If it fails, give a direction that breaks it.

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item $x_1 = 0$: the constraint $x_1 \ge 0$ is \textbf{active}. $x_2 = \val{D1.params.x.2} > 0$: the constraint $x_2 \ge 0$ is inactive, with room on both sides.
  \item The feasible directions are $\val{D1.tex.cone}$, with $s_2$ free. If $s_1 < 0$, then $x_1 + \alpha s_1 < 0$ for every $\alpha > 0$. If $s_1 \ge 0$, the first coordinate stays nonnegative, and $x_2 + \alpha s_2 > 0$ for all $\alpha \in [0, \alpha_0]$, for example with $\alpha_0 = 1/|s_2|$ when $s_2 < 0$ (any $\alpha_0 > 0$ works when $s_2 \ge 0$).
  \item $\nabla f \equiv \val{D1.steps.grad}$, so the condition to test is $s^\top \nabla f = s_1 + s_2 \ge 0$ for \textbf{every} feasible $s$.
  \item Take $s = \val{D1.steps.s}$: it is feasible, and $s^\top \nabla f = \val{D1.steps.slope} < 0$. The condition fails, so $\val{D1.params.x}$ is not a candidate. Moving down the edge decreases $f$ until the corner $\val{D1.steps.xStar}$ with $f = \val{D1.steps.fStar}$, the true minimizer.
  \item To reject a point, one violating direction is enough; to accept it, every feasible direction must pass. Replacing this infinite check by finitely many multipliers is the idea of the KKT conditions in the next seminar.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
Only $x_1 \ge 0$ is active; the feasible directions are $\val{D1.tex.cone}$; $s = \val{D1.steps.s}$ gives $s^\top \nabla f = \val{D1.steps.slope} < 0$, so $\val{D1.params.x}$ is not a candidate.
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{D2}{A directional derivative, two ways}{The limit definition against $s^\top \nabla f$; rate per unit of $\alpha$ versus per unit of length}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $f(x) = \val{D2.tex.f}$, $x = \val{D2.params.x}$ and $s = \val{D2.params.s}$. \textbf{(a)} Compute $\partial f/\partial s\,(x)$ from the definition, as a limit. \textbf{(b)} Compute it again as $s^\top \nabla f(x)$. \textbf{(c)} Is $s$ a descent direction? \textbf{(d)} Is your number a rate per unit of $\alpha$ or per unit of length?

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item $x + \alpha s = \val{D2.tex.xas}$, so $f(x + \alpha s) = \val{D2.tex.expand} = \val{D2.tex.phi}$, and $f(x) = \val{D2.steps.fx}$ is its value at $\alpha = 0$.
  \item
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(x) = \lim_{\alpha \to 0^+} \frac{f(x + \alpha s) - f(x)}{\alpha} = \lim_{\alpha \to 0^+} \bigl(\val{D2.tex.secant}\bigr) = \val{D2.steps.dirDeriv}.
\]
 The limit is one-sided because at a boundary point only $\alpha \ge 0$ may be allowed; at this interior point both one-sided limits agree.
  \item $\nabla f = \val{D2.tex.grad}$, so $\nabla f(x) = \val{D2.steps.grad}$ and $s^\top \nabla f(x) = \val{D2.tex.dot} = \val{D2.steps.dirDeriv}$: both routes agree.
  \item The value is negative, so $s$ is a descent direction. But $\|s\| = \val{D2.tex.normS}$, so $\val{D2.steps.dirDeriv}$ is a rate per unit of $\alpha$; per unit of length it is $\val{D2.tex.perLength} \approx \val{D2.steps.perLength}$.
  \item The steepest descent direction is $-\nabla f(x)/\|\nabla f(x)\|$, with the rate $-\|\nabla f(x)\| = \val{D2.tex.steepest} \approx \val{D2.steps.steepest}$ per unit of length, $\val{D2.tex.ratio} \approx \val{D2.steps.ratio}$ times the rate along $s/\|s\|$. This is why descent methods step against the gradient.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
$f(x + \alpha s) = \val{D2.tex.phi}$, both routes give $\val{D2.steps.dirDeriv}$ per unit of $\alpha$; per unit of length $\val{D2.tex.perLength}$; $s$ is a descent direction.
\end{answerbox}

% =====================================================================
\section{Home practice}\label{sec:home}

Four problems for home: three by hand and one in code. Each is followed by its complete solution, so try it on your own first.

\problemhead{H1}{A singular but nonzero Hessian}{By hand}
\textbf{Statement.} Find the stationary points of $f(x) = \val{home.H1.tex.f}$ and classify them.

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item $\nabla f = \val{home.H1.tex.grad} = 0$ only at the origin.
  \item $H(x) = \val{home.H1.tex.H}$, so $H(0) = \val{home.H1.steps.H0}$ with eigenvalues $\val{home.H1.steps.eig.1}$ and $\val{home.H1.steps.eig.2}$: positive semidefinite, not definite. The necessary condition holds, the sufficient one does not apply.
  \item Along $x_2 = 0$: $f(t, 0) = t^3$ changes sign, so the origin is neither a minimum nor a maximum. Compare with B3: there $H(0) = 0$; here $H(0)$ is not the zero matrix but singular, and the conclusion is the same.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
The only stationary point is the origin; $H(0)$ has eigenvalues $\val{home.H1.steps.eig.1}$ and $\val{home.H1.steps.eig.2}$; neither a minimum nor a maximum.
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{H2}{Minimizers of the quadratic family}{By hand}
\textbf{Statement.} Let $f_a(x) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + a\,x_1x_2$. \textbf{(a)} For $a = \val{home.H2.params.aSelf}$ find the eigenvalues of $H_a$ and the value $f_a\val{home.H2.params.p}$. \textbf{(b)} For which $a$ does $f_a$ have a unique minimizer? \textbf{(c)} Describe all minimizers at $a = \val{home.H2.params.aEdge}$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item The characteristic polynomial is $\val{home.H2.tex.charPoly}$, so the eigenvalues are $2 \pm a$. At $a = \val{home.H2.params.aSelf}$ they are $\val{home.H2.steps.eigSelf.1}$ and $\val{home.H2.steps.eigSelf.2}$, and $f_a\val{home.H2.params.p} = \val{home.H2.steps.value} < 0 = f_a(0)$. Since $f_a(t\,x) = t^2 f_a(x)$, along that direction $f_a$ decreases without bound.
  \item $|a| < \val{home.H2.params.aEdge}$: $H_a \succ 0$, $f_a$ is strictly convex and the origin is the unique minimizer. $|a| > \val{home.H2.params.aEdge}$: $H_a$ is indefinite and $f_a$ is unbounded below, so there is no minimizer.
  \item $a = \val{home.H2.params.aEdge}$: $f = \val{home.H2.tex.fEdge} \ge 0$, and the minimizers are the whole line $x_1 + x_2 = 0$ (for $a = -\val{home.H2.params.aEdge}$, the line $x_1 = x_2$).
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
At $a = \val{home.H2.params.aSelf}$: eigenvalues $\val{home.H2.steps.eigSelf.1}$ and $\val{home.H2.steps.eigSelf.2}$, $f_a\val{home.H2.params.p} = \val{home.H2.steps.value}$. A unique minimizer exactly for $|a| < \val{home.H2.params.aEdge}$; at $a = \val{home.H2.params.aEdge}$ the minimizers form the line $x_1 + x_2 = 0$.
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{H3}{Feasible directions at a corner}{By hand}
\textbf{Statement.} For $\Omega = \{x:\ x_1 \ge 0,\ x_2 \ge 0\}$ and $f(x) = \val{D1.tex.f}$, describe the feasible directions at $x = \val{home.H3.params.x}$ and check the first-order necessary condition there.

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item Both constraints are active, so the feasible directions are $\{s \ne 0:\ s_1 \ge 0,\ s_2 \ge 0\}$.
  \item $s^\top \nabla f = s_1 + s_2 > 0$ for every such $s$: the condition holds. Over unit feasible directions the smallest rate is $\val{home.H3.steps.minSlope}$, attained along the edges.
  \item Indeed $f \ge 0$ on $\Omega$ and $f = 0$ at the corner, so the corner is the minimizer. Compare with D1, where one inactive constraint left room for the violating direction.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
Both constraints are active; the feasible directions are $s \ne 0$ with $s_1 \ge 0$ and $s_2 \ge 0$; the condition holds, and the corner is the minimizer.
\end{answerbox}

\problemhead{H4}{The second-order test in code}{In code}
\textbf{Statement.} Using \texttt{classify} from block B, test the Hessians of today at their points: A1, A2 at $\val{A2.params.x}$, A3, B1, B2, B3 and B4 at the origin, C2, H1 at the origin and the pair $\operatorname{diag}(0, -1)$, $\operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$. Where does it answer \texttt{"inconclusive"}, and why does A2 get \texttt{"min"}?

\textbf{Solution.}
\begingroup\sloppy
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*]
  \item Build each Hessian exactly (by hand or with \texttt{sympy}) as a \texttt{numpy} array and call \texttt{classify(H)}.
  \item The labels: \val{home.H4.counts.min} times \texttt{"min"} (A1, A2, A3, B1), \val{home.H4.counts.saddle} times \texttt{"saddle"} (B2, C2) and \val{home.H4.counts.inconclusive} times \texttt{"inconclusive"} (B3, B4, H1 and both diagonal matrices).
  \item None of the \texttt{"inconclusive"} answers is a bug: the second-order test genuinely cannot decide there. The version with the chained comparison \texttt{w.min() < -tol < w.max()} calls $\operatorname{diag}(0, -1)$ a saddle; the test must require a negative \textbf{and} a positive eigenvalue. A Hessian computed by finite differences is another matter: for B4 at the origin it is a tiny positive diagonal matrix, and \texttt{classify} answers \texttt{"min"}; no tolerance rule can tell an exact zero from a tiny positive number without a scale taken from the problem.
  \item A2 gets \texttt{"min"} because \texttt{classify} reads the matrix only: $H\val{A2.params.x} \succ 0$, but the point is not stationary, so the label means nothing there.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
\begin{answerbox}
\texttt{"inconclusive"} for B3, B4, H1, $\operatorname{diag}(0, -1)$ and $\operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$; A2 gets \texttt{"min"} because the function reads $H$ only and the point is not stationary.
\end{answerbox}

\section{Common mistakes}\label{sec:mistakes}

Mistakes that come up again and again: first by topic, then from the seminar problems.

\subsection{Gradients and Hessians}\label{sub:mistakes-a}

\begin{itemize}[label=\textcolor{hseaccent}{\textbullet}]
  \item A cross term $c\,x_ix_j$ puts $c$ into both $H_{ij}$ and $H_{ji}$. Writing $c/2$ (the entry of $A$ in $f = x^\top A x$) or doubling $c$ as on the diagonal gives a wrong Hessian.
  \item Discussing the Hessian at a point before checking $\nabla f = 0$ there: at a non-stationary point $H \succ 0$ means nothing for optimality.
  \item Treating the Hessian of a cubic as constant: only a quadratic has the same $H$ at every point.
\end{itemize}

From the problems:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{A1.} Writing $-2$ off the diagonal (doubling the cross coefficient as on the diagonal) or $-\tfrac12$ (the entry of $A$ in $f = x^\top A x$), or putting $-1$ into only one of the two entries.
  \item \textbf{A1.} Discussing optimality at $\val{A1.params.x}$ from the Hessian: the gradient is not zero there.
  \item \textbf{A2.} Losing a sign: at $x_2 < 0$ both off-diagonal entries are negative, and $\partial f/\partial x_2$ is a sum of two negative terms.
  \item \textbf{A2.} Announcing a minimum because $H \succ 0$ at a point where $\nabla f \ne 0$.
  \item \textbf{A3.} Halving the cross coefficients, or writing each of them into only one of the two symmetric entries.
  \item \textbf{A3.} Calling the stationary point a global minimum without an argument: here it is convexity, from $H \succ 0$ at every point.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Classifying stationary points}\label{sub:mistakes-b}

\begin{itemize}[label=\textcolor{hseaccent}{\textbullet}]
  \item Concluding “indefinite” because neither Sylvester pattern holds: $\operatorname{diag}(0, -1)$ and $\operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$ have the same leading minors, yet the first is negative semidefinite and the second positive semidefinite.
  \item Reading the necessary condition $H(x^*) \succeq 0$ as a certificate: $H = 0$ holds at the monkey saddle, which has no extremum.
  \item Claiming a global minimum from $\nabla f = 0$ and $H \succ 0$: the sufficient condition gives a strict local minimum only.
  \item Offering a contour picture as the proof of a saddle: restrictions to lines are the proof.
\end{itemize}

From the problems:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{B1.} Claiming a global minimum from $H(x^*) \succ 0$ alone.
  \item \textbf{B2.} Offering the contour picture as the proof; it is only a guide.
  \item \textbf{B3.} Concluding a minimum from $H(0) = 0 \succeq 0$: that treats the necessary condition as if it were sufficient. This is the mistake the problem exists for.
  \item \textbf{B3.} Testing only the $x_2$-axis, where $f \equiv 0$, and concluding that nothing happens.
  \item \textbf{B4.} Calling the silent test “bad luck”: with $H$ singular and semidefinite, the first- and second-order data cannot separate B3 from B4.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Convexity}\label{sub:mistakes-c}

\begin{itemize}[label=\textcolor{hseaccent}{\textbullet}]
  \item Judging convexity of a quadratic by the sign of the cross term: its size decides.
  \item Confusing convexity with smoothness: the $\ell_1$ diamond has corners and is convex, the ring has a smooth boundary and is not.
  \item Proving convexity with a drawing or with a few segments that stay inside: only a proof for all pairs counts.
\end{itemize}

From the problems:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{C1.} Giving a drawing instead of a proof, or a chain of inequalities without the reason for each step.
  \item \textbf{C2.} Judging by the sign of the cross term: A1 and C2 both have a negative one.
  \item \textbf{C2.} Concluding “indefinite” only because neither Sylvester pattern holds: the negative determinant is what proves it here.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Feasible directions}\label{sub:mistakes-d}

\begin{itemize}[label=\textcolor{hseaccent}{\textbullet}]
  \item Declaring every direction feasible at a boundary point, or none.
  \item Accepting a boundary point after checking a few directions: rejecting needs one violating direction, accepting needs all of them.
  \item Comparing directional derivatives of directions with different lengths: normalize first, or the longest direction looks the steepest.
\end{itemize}

From the problems:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{D1.} Declaring all directions feasible, or none.
  \item \textbf{D1.} Testing only directions that point into the interior and concluding that the condition holds.
  \item \textbf{D2.} Reporting $\val{D2.steps.dirDeriv}$ as the rate per unit of length: $s$ is not a unit vector.
  \item \textbf{D2.} Forgetting to subtract $f(x)$ before dividing by $\alpha$: the quotient $f(x + \alpha s)/\alpha$ has no finite limit.
\end{itemize}

\section{Glossary}\label{sec:glossary}

The English terms of the seminar with short meanings and their Russian equivalents.

\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.66\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Term} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
optimization problem & finding the smallest value of a function over a set \\
objective function & the function being minimized; in machine learning, the loss \\
empirical risk & the average loss of a model over the training data \\
feasible set & the set of points among which the minimum is sought \\
interior point & a point that lies in the set together with a small ball around it \\
boundary point & a point of the set with points outside the set arbitrarily close to it \\
local minimum & a point with the smallest value among all nearby feasible points \\
global minimum & a point with the smallest value on the whole feasible set \\
strict minimum & a minimum where every other admissible point gives a strictly larger value \\
minimizer & the point at which a minimum is attained \\
stationary point & a point where the gradient is zero \\
saddle point & a stationary point that is neither a minimum nor a maximum \\
monkey saddle & a saddle with three descending sectors instead of two \\
level set & the set of points where a function takes a given value \\
partial derivative & the derivative with respect to one variable while the others are fixed \\
gradient & the column vector of all first partial derivatives \\
Hessian & the matrix of all second partial derivatives \\
directional derivative & the rate of change of a function when moving from a point along a direction \\
descent direction & a direction along which the function decreases to first order \\
steepest descent direction & the direction opposite to the gradient \\
Taylor's formula & the approximation of a smooth function near a point by a polynomial \\
quadratic form & the number h transpose A h for a symmetric matrix A and a vector h \\
cross term & a product of two different variables with a coefficient \\
eigenvalue & the stretching factor of a matrix along one of its eigenvectors \\
positive definite matrix & a symmetric matrix whose quadratic form is positive for every nonzero vector \\
positive semidefinite matrix & a symmetric matrix whose quadratic form is nonnegative for every vector \\
indefinite matrix & a symmetric matrix whose quadratic form takes both signs \\
determinant & the number ad - bc of a two by two matrix, and the product of the eigenvalues in general \\
leading principal minor & the determinant of the upper-left square block of a matrix \\
principal minor & the determinant on a set of rows and the same set of columns \\
Sylvester's criterion & a symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when all its leading principal minors are positive \\
necessary condition & a condition that every minimum satisfies; its failure rules a point out \\
sufficient condition & a condition that guarantees a minimum \\
feasible direction & a direction in which a small step keeps the point in the feasible set \\
active constraint & an inequality that holds with equality at the point \\
convex set & a set that contains the segment between any two of its points \\
convex function & a function whose graph lies on or below each of its chords \\
strictly convex function & a convex function for which the chord inequality is strict between distinct points \\
condition number & the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of a positive definite matrix \\
central difference & an estimate of a derivative from the values of a function at two points symmetric around the given one \\
tolerance & the threshold below which a computed number is treated as zero \\
\end{longtable}
